MR. CHURCHILL-CHANGE IN "HANSARD" BY DEFENCE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a point of order-I think this is the proper time to do it-with regard to an alteration which has been made in Hansard without the authority of the House of Commons. I refer to page 6140, the second column. Yesterday I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) a supplementary question which reads:
Does he not think he should place greater emphasis on the fighting efficiency of our armed services rather than on the building of a monument in stone to himself?
The Minister of National Defence replied in these words, which I heard and which were recorded by the Hansard reporter and reproduced on the blues: "Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the emphasis that I want". The minister has now, without the authority of the House of Commons, struck out the word "that" and put in a phrase which he does not understand and which he never used- "fighting efficiency".
My point of order is this. I would ask Your Honour to rule that revised Hansard should carry the original version of this statement, because we are not entitled to make changes in substance. I am quite aware that ministers of the crown in answer to questions may give no reply at all or may make stupid answers, but they are not entitled to make up for their intellectual deficiencies by changing the substance of Hansard.

Mr. Chairman, last evening I mentioned an example of gross and unjustifiable expenditure in the proposal to build a defence headquarters in Ottawa when in every part of this nation the construction industry is being asked to withhold and postpone construction. With the reduction in the number of men in the armed forces and as a consequence a pronounced drop in morale, this expenditure is one of those things that cannot in any way be justified. I am waiting to hear the explanation from the Minister of Public Works as to the estimate for the cost of Canada's Pentagon, for at the time the announcement was made the press all over this nation was under the impression that the expenditure would be over $100 million.
Whether it is $35 million, $50 million or $100 million, this is something that is not needed. Certainly provision will have to be made for better accommodation for those in the Department of National Defence than they have had over the years; but this is no time, when the Canadian taxpayer is being taxed as never before, to engage in measures that can only have as their purpose the adulation of the minister who presides over the department.
Having said that-

I welcome the minister's interruption because it indicates that he too is feeling the heat of controversy. Only yesterday the hon. member for Davenport, in the course of the educational campaign which he now wages across the country, asked that a criminal offence be placed on the statute books of the nation in respect of contributions received from foreign corporations.

election, he might be able to tell us whether the reason for his sudden dislike of United States assistance is based on considerations that were not in his mind in the elections of 1962 and 1963.
I would like the minister to let us know how things have been going in regard to the difference of opinion between himself and the former minister. Many have said there is a widespread division between them. I do not believe it. They are fighting with powderpuffs. The Minister of Finance says he does not agree with everything that the member for Davenport advances. He believes that in Canada we must maintain a strong spirit in support of Canadian investment by Canadians. On the other hand, the hon. member for Davenport says that the "friendly giant" has evil designs on us-I use his words-and he is afraid we are going to be smothered and swallowed up. This is very strange, Mr. Chairman, because it was that gentleman who, in July of 1963 and again in July of 1965, flew to Washington and signed agreements tying Canada's fiscal policies to the United States of America's balance of payments problem. It was he who, having bitterly protested against allowing United States banking concerns to obtain a foothold in Canada, acted contrary to his public declarations. We would therefore like to know what is the political philosophy followed by the present government with relation to United States investment.
I will not quote from the many press references that have been made but I do think I should refer to something that indicates the feeling of the people of the United States. It is set out in the issue of U.S. News & World Report of May 30 and reads as follows:
Once again, Canadians are getting in a mood to try to declare their economic independence from the United States.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Suddenly a period of uncertainty appears to lie ahead for U.S. investors in Canada and for U.S. companies with Canadian subsidiaries.
The article goes on to state that a book has been published by the hon. member for Davenport, "A Choice For Canada". If one may summarize, the book outlines certain steps that should be taken such as lower depreciation write-offs for foreign owned subsidiaries than for domestic companies. Does the minister accept the philosophy inherent in that statement. There is the suggestion of a withholding tax on management and professional

fees for non-residents. Does the minister, having inherited the garments of the hon. member for Davenport, accept that principle? The book says that there should be a tax on stock transfers of Canadian firms which become foreign owned. Does the Minister of Finance accept the tutelage of his predecessor? There is a suggestion of customs duties to prevent foreign subsidiaries from increasing their imports from foreign firms. Is that basic principle of the predecessor of the present minister now being considered? It is suggested there should be non-deductible interest charges for corporate tax purposes on new borrowings by foreign owned subsidiaries.
I ask these questions because Canadians are wondering what the attitude of the present government is. The Minister of Finance made a speech in Toronto in which he reviewed the ten steps to economic greatness. In these ten steps there are indications that several of the principles of the hon. member for Davenport have been accepted by the present government. All we would like to know is, what are the views of the present government on the subject of foreign investment? So far as we are concerned, we have always taken the stand that foreign investment is welcome and will not be interfered with but that investment in Canada shall act in the interests of Canada in the determination of policies.
This was called anti-Americanism. What are the views of the present government? I ask that because there have been some amazing changes. Let me refer to the Canada Development Corporation. At one time it was r.ot looked upon favourably by the Minister of Finance. Later there was lukewarm approval and now this infant, yet to be born, has received a degree of approval from the Minister of Finance which would indicate that the doctrine of the former minister has taken hold. Unless the minister gives the house a full and complete answer-not in some club in Toronto but in the House of Commons-I shall have something more to say.
The general attitude of the press across the country indicates that the battle between these two giants is not a sham fight. I think it is. However, the question asked across the country has been summarized well in the Vancouver Province. This newspaper says that the basic policy difference between the Minister of Finance and his predecessor, Walter Gordon, is now well understood. Both

Mr. Chairman, under the present resolution concerning the income tax, I feel it is appropriate to remind the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) about the change in administration which took place recently in "la belle province" of Quebec. I do not know whether the minister has had the opportunity to obtain and read the substantial political platform of the Union Na-tionale which will soon-in a few hours-be sanctioned, but I think it is time for him to get hold of it, seeing that it contains many planks relating to the income tax.
Among other things, and this is not a new fiscal policy, the National Union government

since its formation seeks 100 per cent of individual income tax, corporation tax and death duties. There is nothing revolutionary or reprehensible in this position, far from it, Mr. Chairman. It is basically constitutional, in accordance with the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution of 1867.
When this new Quebec government claims 100 per cent of direct taxes, including among others, the income tax, the tax on corporations and death duties, the claim is based on paragraph (2) of section 92 of the constitution, which allocates exclusively to the provinces, the direct taxes levied in such province for provincial purposes. Clearly, when the economy of the Canadian constitution is perused, it appears that section 91, paragraph (3) allows the central government to levy taxes in the country through taxation, but when direct taxes levied in a province for provincial purposes are involved, section 91 should be read along with section 92. It is clearly indicated that a province, any of the Canadian provinces, has exclusive rights in matters of direct taxation for provincial purposes.
An exclusive right is not one which another government can seize, or take over at leisure to remit later, bit by bit, in various circumstances. An exclusive right is one that belongs to a province in an absolute and sovereign manner, and which a province may, of its own free will, share with the central government or with any province.
Now, the government of the province of Quebec has clearly expressed, in its substantial platform, during the election campaign, its intention to take over, not to beg, as Mr. Daniel Johnson has just stated, in other words, simply to occupy the fields of taxation in the proportion 100, 100 and 100.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This is not a revolutionary procedure. I would not want anyone to think in this house and in other provinces, that this is intended to sabotage the Canadian confederation, far from it. Besides, this is entirely within the spirit in which the Canadian confederation was founded, that is the principle of responsible government, which had been granted earlier in 1847, and which was embodied in the wording of the Canadian constitution, requires that any government administering a territory-be it national or provincial-is accountable to its constituents. To give accounts, it must be in a position to have its own taxation income, to collect for itself the taxes which are devolved onto it.
June 9, 1966

Many politicians in the house have asserted the principle that it is harmful and inadmissible that a government such as the central government, for example, should levy direct taxes, hand them over to the province as it pleases, and that another government should spend that money.
In view of this theory or responsible government, I believe the hon. Minister of Finance should look into the event which has just taken place in the province of Quebec before a conflict erupts and government pressures are applied.
That is why, since the beginning of the present session, many members on both sides of the house have stood up to request that the government establish a joint parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution as a first step towards a national conference on the Canadian constitution.
I wonder why, in the face of so many proper requests and just pleas to serve the common good of the country, the present government still hesitates and displays inertia or indifference. There is a need not only for political, constitutional, cultural or other reforms, but also for a fiscal reform adapted to the economic and fiscal problems of 1966, and all this is absolutely urgent.
These last few years the province of Quebec has established within its legislature a parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution, precisely in order to be more specific concerning these particular reforms. But in Ottawa, the country is administered haphazardly; as a matter of fact, the government is even preparing further encroachments in fields entirely under provincial jurisdiction, without having obtained beforehand the consent of the province or provinces concerned, or without having fully discussed the matter with them, although they object to it. This is very bad for the country, Mr. Chairman.
I am convinced that if Canadians across the country were to undertake this dialogue in good faith and not as we are now going about it, these problems would be settled, since they are primarily material problems, and this would help solve the psychological problem affecting all Canadians, from one ocean to the other.
I hope the Minister of Finance will use his influence within the cabinet, not only in the field of foreign investments in Canada, but also in the settlement of this important problem which has now become more urgent with
Income Tax Act
the recent change of government in the province of Quebec, in order to institute a joint parliamentary committee in Ottawa so that the legislators of the country, in the Senate and the House of Commons, may establish a dialogue.
A large number of studies and reports are made available to us, but we should first come to an understanding if we are to reach a final agreement with the other provinces at a national conference on the constitution.
When such things are said I am reminded of a scene in the Bible. In the three months I have been here, each time an hon. member raised that urgent, substantial and capital question, he looked to me a little like Saint John the Baptist preaching in the desert.
Frankly, the reactions of the present government are very disappointing. This government should not have any illusions on that point; it will not solve the country's fiscal and political problems by going on like that, in short by governing without any planning, any definite goals, and by taking over provincial fields of jurisdiction. Of course, once it has taken over a field, it intends to open a dialogue with the provinces; but it does so belatedly when it is already deeply involved on the administrative side.
Recently, we saw the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) postpone the conference on education. Of course, the federal government knows that the new government of the province of Quebec, that of the National Union, is exclusively provincial, free of direct or indirect ties with a great national party, dedicated to the prime interests of Quebec, fundamentally autonomist on fiscal matters. The Ottawa government knows very well that it will have to revise its position if it wants a constructive atmosphere to exist throughout the country, especially in the fiscal field.
Therefore, once again I ask the Minister of Finance to give that program a structure. It is important to say it and to take that matter seriously; that party is not called the Liberal party. I will remind the minister that in the province of Quebec there are many very intelligent Liberals who vote for the National Union. It is therefore important that it should study that program with regard to fiscal matters and revise and adapt its national fiscal programs to take into account the particular requirements of the province of Quebec which, as far as I know, is not trying in any way to pick a quarrel with the rest of the country but rather to meet the particular aspirations of its constituents.

There is also another thing in the program of the National Union government, namely the basic income tax exemption of $4,000 for married people and $2,000 for single people.
This new government promised to grant this tax exemption during its very first session. This provincial tax exemption will have consequences which will create pressures and tensions, if the federal government does not consider following the example of the Quebec government in that direction.
Not only the people of the province of Quebec want that, but all Canadians, the popular mass, the working class, the small businessman, the person who works in an office, the young woman, the married woman, the widow. The mass of the Canadian people find it difficult, due to the fiscal burden, to provide for their needs.
If it is not the only method, it is at least a first step to put up a good fight against poverty in our country.
There are in Sherbrooke especially many textile industries where workers are now on strike. I hope that the conflict will be settled as soon as possible. These workers earn about $60 a week and many of them have three, five, six or seven children. It is unthinkable, Mr. Chairman, to provide for all needs, considering such a heavy tax burden, even with this small cut of about six cents a week that the Minister of Finance has deigned to grant this category of taxpayers.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
In order to work with love, hope and warmth, it is therefore necessary that these Canadians, married or unmarried and earning less that $4,000 or $2,000 respectively, shall be exempt from income tax. That is what the Quebec government is going to do and that is why the Minister of Finance should give consideration to a similar adjustment and if he does so, I feel he will rate the admiration and friendship of millions of Canadians. When it is said, by him or by other ministers, in the house or elsewhere, that a campaign against poverty is being waged, then those millions of Canadians will say: The speeches are over, something is now being done.
I should also like to call the attention of the minister to other things. Various industries, businesses and trades may deduct from their income tax returns a certain amount for administrative expenses. It is an excellent thing to promote the development of trade and industry.

But there is a class of Canadians, and these are, for instance, the millions of workers who are required to buy, and pay out of their meager salary, their tool kits and $400 or $500 worth of tools, without which they could not keep their jobs. It is absolutely essential for them to have their tools to practise their special trade. The companies and the employers do not supply to their employees these numerous and very expensive tools.
Now, I think this point should be considered, that some percentage, to be determined by the experts in the minister's department, should be allowed as a deduction for such tools as the workers are required to purchase to practise their trade, to earn their living and that of their families.
Something else is occasionally brought to my attention; I do not know if the grievance is well founded. It seems that in some provinces government taxes are collected by merchants and businessmen. I am told this is the case in Quebec, where the government gives a certain commission to the merchants and businessmen who collect for it certain indirect taxes. Why, therefore, could the federal government not give some kind of a commission to Canadians who do its work, who after a fashion are its employees, its representatives?
Mr. Chairman, to bring these few remarks to a close I would like to say this: I wish the practice of preventing us from getting a reply to our questions during the question period, were put to an end in the house. We should not permit that no reply be allowed. Not that I question the authority of Mr. Speaker whom I greatly respect; but, on the other hand, he does not hold his authority from God but from members of the house, individually and jointly. I believe it is important, even urgent, that the tax problem take this into consideration. Now, how should we put it? In three languages, six languages? Should it be put calmly or in furious tones? When oh, when will the present government institute, during this session, a parliamentary committee to study the Canadian constitution, so that neither in this house nor in the other the trend of thought be allowed to go in opposite directions since it could easily be channeled into one direction if representatives had a chance to gather about a table, so that we, Canadians, who are brothers from sea to sea, might solve the problems of our country.
June 9, 1966

How much misunderstanding there is, because we let this persist and because we tolerate a kind of vacuum that prevents Canadians from sea to sea, nay, in this house and in the other place, from joining together. There are no problems in the House of Commons, when we are talking to representatives from Newfoundland, Nova Scotia or the west. On the other hand, there is a fundamental problem and that is the problem of the revision, the adjustment of the political, constitutional, fiscal, economic and cultural problems when the provinces-not only Quebec, but British Columbia, Manitoba and Ontario-each in their own way, claim to have fiscal jurisdiction, some larger than others, and economic responsibilities. Yet the present government remains in such a constitutional and political disorder. Well, I believe the country is not being served by a refusal to form a parliament committee. I hope that very soon, the Minister of Finance, who seems to be a most charming man, will use his influence to bring the government around to this decision and then we will be given the opportunity to face the Quebec parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution.

Dear Mr. Herridge:
I have received your letter dated May 4 enclosing a copy of a letter and additional material from Mr. J. D. McDonald, chairman of the Rossland centennial project asking if exemption from federal sales tax could be provided for materials used in the construction of centennial projects.
Requests that a sales tax exemption be provided for materials used in all centennial projects have been carefully studied but it was decided that federal assistance in this form would be very unfair since the proportion of the total cost of projects attributable to sales tax would vary widely from project to project and thus from municipality to municipality. Moreover, since the federal sales tax is paid at the time manufacturers sell their products it would be very difficult to administer an exemption from this tax for goods purchased from wholesalers and retailers for use in thousands of centennial projects across Canada. It was decided that a better way for the federal government to make its contribution would be by grants for the assistance of commemorative community projects.
Yours sincerely,
Mitchell Sharp

June 9, 1966
Income Tax Act
I sent a copy of that letter to Mr. McDonald and he brought it to the attention of the Rossland Committee and various organizations. 1 might say that I am not presenting my argument as a socialist. As a matter of fact, this argument is being advanced by quite a number of organizations in the district I have the honour to represent who agree with the philosophy of the minister so far as our system is concerned. However, they think that in this case there is some inconsistency.
I sent the minister's letter to Mr. McDonald and I received a reply from him which I will read since I think the minister will be interested in his suggestions. He wrote:
Dear Sir:
Thank you lor your letter of May 18th enclosing Hon. Mitchell Sharp's reply to our request for sales tax exemption on centennial projects. His information was placed before the centennial committee at our May 25th meeting. The committee expressed disappointment that these projects are not sales tax exempt. As requested, we offer the following comments regarding Mr. Sharp's letter:
1.	Whereas Mr. Sharp suggests that the removal of sales tax would in effect constitute extra federal assistance to those communities whose projects include a building as opposed to projects that do not, we believe that just the opposite is true. We suggest that it is the imposition of the sales tax that creates the inequality. Our reasoning is as follows: federal centennial grants are allotted on an equal basis of $1 per capita regardless of the size of the project. Now a community whose project does not involve purchase of building materials is able to retain the full per capita dollar to be spent on the project. On the other hand, a community whose project requires purchase of building materials must turn part of that per capita dollar back to the federal government in the form of sales tax. This is where the true inequality lies. Removal of the sales tax would remove this inequality by allowing all communities to have the use of the full per capita dollar regardless of their choice of project.
2.	Mr. Sharp also suggests that it would be difficult to administer the sales tax exemption for centennial projects. We are informed that sales tax exemption is successfully adminstered for hospital construction and we cannot understand why it would be any more difficult in the case of a centennial project building.
3.	We would repeat our previous observation that to ensure the success of Canada's centennial year, the federal government has asked the municipalities to undertake these projects. Of necessity, the projects must be financed with donated funds and in the case of the Rossland project, the response has been gratifying. It does not make good sense that the government should jeodardize the ultimate success of these projects by funnelling off a portion of this donated money for sales tax.
Your very truly,
J. D. McDonald Chairman.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that I think Mr. McDonald, who is a well known figure in the district, has a very convincing argument, at least from my point of view. I wish to bring to the minister's attention again that this is the point of view of practically every committee that is undertaking a centennial project in my constituency.
In conclusion I wish to ask the minister to take another look at this matter to see if some way cannot be found to remove the inequality arising from the minister's decision and mentioned in Mr. McDonald's comments on the minister's reply.

Mr. Chairman, as I was not
in the house yesterday, having gone with the other members to visit Expo '67, I missed a good part of the debate; consequently, I may repeat what some other members have already said, for which I apologize ahead of time. I have a few remarks to make to the minister with regard to income tax.
In his amendment on income tax the minister first tries, as is the case with all other legislation anyway, to give a tidbit to the taxpayers. He tells us that, for the coming years, if the house so decides:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:
1. That for the 1967 and subsequent taxation years the deduction from individual income tax equal to the lesser of 10 per cent of basic tax or $600, described in subsection (4) of section 33 of the said act, be replaced by a deduction equal to the lesser of 20 per cent of basic tax or $20, and that for the 1966 taxation year the deduction be equal to the aggregate of
(a) 4 per cent of basic tax or $240, whichever is the lesser-
Etc., etc.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
"Whichever is the lesser". It is obvious that if one starts reading the Income Tax Act, one merely finds the nicest labyrinth in expressions, designed to confuse the taxpayer to the extent that he understands nothing. And all that for what?
That reminds me of last year's reduction when the minister came up with a 10 per cent reduction on income tax. The day after, all newspapers flashed headlines two inches wide: '10 per cent tax cut". In fact, that meant about nothing, just like what is brought forward today. What does it mean? In order to enlighten dazzled taxpayers a bit, what does it mean in terms of dollars?

June 9, 1966

Take a family man, with his wife and two children, who earns $3,000 per year. Before, with last year's reduction, he would have paid $22. Now, he will pay $20. He gets a $2 gift. Imagine. What a gift for a family man: $2 at the end of the year. Another, who earned $3,500, paid $58, compared to $53 this year, a saving of $5. That is the highest cut the government will grant with the amendment to the act.
To take so long to conceive such an aberration.
One who earns $4,000 previously paid $100; he will now pay $97 and thus save $3 this year. One who earns $7,000 paid last year $199, but he will now pay $205. This is the beginning, the government is gaining; after having given $2, $3 or $5, it is now collecting from others $6 more. One who earns $5,500 and who paid $519, will now pay $554, that is $35 more. When $1 is given to a taxpayer, $10 or $15 are deducted from another. This is a huge joke. It is exactly that joke, Mr. Chairman, which everyone finds sickening. We are told nowadays that we have separatists and rebels. What is the cause of that rebellion throughout the country. Such sordid measures as those introduced by the government.
People are convinced that administrators are working all day long to try to fool the taxpayer. And for whose benefit? For the benefit of capitalists and bankers.
I have drawn up the picture. Last year there was a $10 reduction for a taxpayer who paid $100 in income tax; this year, there will be a $2 or $3 reduction.
I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that if we consider the legislation from the taxpayer's point of view, it is rather poor. The legislation now in force will still encourage large companies, foreign capital, and Canadians will be invited to go and borrow abroad, even in Europe.
I read in the newspaper which I have here: Steps to facilitate loans in Europe
The municipal, provincial and federal authorities will be able to borrow abroad more easily-
You will notice that is the key word:
-following the abolition of the 15 per cent tax which non-residents in Canada must pay on interest on Canadian government bonds.
This exemption, which will come into effect on April 15, is to facilitate the sale of debentures and bonds to the United States and Europe and allow all three levels of government to obtain more easily the money necessary to cover the cost of public services.
Income Tax Act
This is what we do here in the House of Commons; we pass all sorts of laws to try to attract foreign capital for the development of Canada. Those among us who could invest some money in government securities do not have these advantages. These people are charged 100 per cent and every piece of legislation seeks to empty their pockets. Then they are told: Go ahead and invest. They are taxed to the last penny and then told: Invest; you do not invest, we have to seek foreign capital.
Mr. Chairman, if foreign capital is sought, it is because the government wants to bring these huge amounts into the country.
I am not against bringing in foreign capital. We are not against this influx, but we feel it is dangerous to offer these special conditions to foreign capital.
Already today we feel the Canadian economy is increasingly slipping under foreign control. We belong to foreigners in a proportion of 80 per cent and the more it goes on, the worse it gets. If we continue to encourage foreign capital to the detriment of Canadian investors, there is no doubt that we will have at a given time, to backtrack and pay more attention to Canadian capital, to those who would like to invest money and who are afraid to do so now. Indeed, if a Canadian wants today to invest his money in public or government undertakings, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) is watching so as to tax him. How do you want these people to invest Canadian capital in this country's undertakings? It is impossible.
As I said, as long as foreign capital is favoured like that, our economy will be shaky and will fall more and more every day into the hands of foreign owners. What we are asking the minister to do, if some legislation can be introduced to amend the Income Tax Act, is to improve the exemptions with regard to tools used by wage-earners. That is what I asked for in the house and forest workers are also asking for an exemption for the cost of their tools. An exemption is granted to the big companies for machinery; they are exempt from income tax. Why should we not exempt a worker who must today get a power-saw, buy modern equipment often worth $500, $600 or $700 to work in the bush. That worker should get an income tax exemption.
Then we will start working on a popular basis to help the taxpayer. Why not also exempt his transportation costs, his living expenses and even his vacation travelling

expenses. Why not? Why should a worker be treated differently than a businessman, an industrialist? I am a businessman and I have the right to deduct for income tax purposes all expenses related to my business. I am fully entitled to do so and why do we deny the worker that right? The Income Tax Act is truly unfair in that respect, especially if we really want to help the taxpayer. When he introduced his legislation, the Minister of Finance said that it was to help the small wage-earner. An exemption of $2 per year, then $5, will not help him very much. He will not go far with that. But if the minister had wanted to be sincere, above all serious, he would have increased the basic exemption to $2,000 for unmarried people and to $4,000 for married people.
You will have tomorrow or in the weeks to come the example of the province of Quebec which will finally adopt basic exemptions of $2,000 and $4,000; I hope the federal government will follow suit, that it will follow in the footsteps of the province of Quebec. They might be surer than those of the jokers we Lad before.
Now, we could suggest to the minister to consider also an exemption on family housing, an income tax exemption for the head of a family who has a property on which he must pay taxes. It is said quite rightly that property owners are getting fewer and fewer today. As a matter of fact, it is almost impossible to keep a property with the host of taxes which are levied on it: federal tax, provincial tax, municipal tax, elementary school tax, secondary school tax and university tax.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, how a home owner, the head of a family, will be able to afford the maintenance of his house under such a flood of taxes. It will be utterly impossible and we ask the Minister of Finance to do something for the family house-ing.
Another tax we have never accepted and have never swallowed it the 11 per cent tax on building materials. Here again, they started by disguising the tax. When the 11 per cent tax on building materials was proposed, it was said: A 5 per cent premium will be paid on winter-built houses. A paltry gift of $500 was offered in order to get $1,500 or $2,000 more on the building materials that go into a family dwelling. Well, Mr. Chairman, we want this tax to be removed because

today, strangely enough, the $500 gift has disappeared. It is hardly given anymore, but the well-known 11 per cent tax is still there. If the gift is to be taken away, at least the charge should be removed. The gift is taken away, but we still have the well-known 11 per cent tax to pay.
As far as charitable donations are concerned, more run around, more dilly-dallying. In the past, at every opportunity, we have asked that a standard of, for instance, 10 per cent of a worker's income, be established concerning deductions for charitable donations. Let us stop fooling around with charitable donations and forcing every parish priest to file reports and play detective in the field of charity. That is just a farce. I do not know whether it is inspired by anti-Christians or by people who would fain have Christianity lose its sway over Canada, but today, the legislation is being changed: our rectories are to be collection offices; every parish priest will have to be registered to be able to report and deduct charitable donations for the people who will go and get their receipts at the rectory.
Mr. Chairman, the man who conceived such an idea was probably an outstanding man, but he was surely not a Christian. Had he been a sincere Christian, he would not have done such a thing. I feel it is an indirect and disguised way of making light of religion, of Christianity in general. When I think about charity, religion comes to my mind. I noted that under the amendment proposed earlier, deductions were being allowed for charitable donations to the UN, to Japan, to Russia; however, I was surprised at not finding any provision for the deduction of charitable donations to the Communist party. If deductions of 10 or 15 per cent of the income had simply been allowed for charitable donations, all those endless inquiries and investigations in every rectory and within all Christian organizations would have been prevented.
As for us, French Canadians from Quebec, all we hope for and expect from the Minister of Finance with respect to income tax-I said so on many occasions and I say it again this evening- is that the federal government will hand over to the province of Quebec its three taxation fields, namely: personal income tax, corporate income tax and estate taxes. Afterwards, we shall be in a position to exchange views in a spirit of justice here in Ottawa.
June 9, 1966

I know that the present government has promised many times to hand over those three taxation fields; but nothing has been done yet. Everybody is amazed today to see what is going on in the province of Quebec. Lesage was quite a surprise for everyone. This is no surprise.
Quebec wants something and will demand it. As the new Quebec premier has put it: We are not going to beg or ask the federal government for charity, we will take what belongs to us.
Regardless of his political affiliation, that is a man after Quebec's heart. I am merely asking the Minister of Finance to work sincerely toward returning to Quebec the three fields of taxation, or all fields of direct taxation which rightfully belong to the provinces. Then, you can be sure that we and the whole of Quebec will be ready to work with all the others provinces for the development of Canada.

Quite frankly it is an experiment, as I mentioned yesterday when I put forward certain amendments that I hope will be proposed in due course.
Some problems had to be dealt with because we were not absolutely certain of the impact of this tax upon the taxpayers. I have proposed certain relieving provisions as a result of representations which have been made.
Undoubtedly the information I have-this is directly in response to the question asked by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition-is that the tax is having its intended effect. It seems to be cutting back moderately on some of the projects that had been planned.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The committee will realize that a great many of the smaller companies in this country will not be subject to the 5 per cent tax because of the floor of $30,000. The tax applies in the main to the larger companies. Some of them will find it both possible and necessary to continue with projects exactly as planned. This is not surprising. We expected it. Others will find it possible and desirable to reduce their projects to a moderate extent. It is not our intention to stop any projects. Our purpose is to cut them down.
As I said yesterday or the day before when I was talking about the excise tax, our objective is only a modest reduction in the scale of capital expenditure, $300 million or $400 million out of $10 billion. We do not want anything to be stopped; what we want are some reductions made in order to ease inflationary pressures. I have no doubt that we shall look back on this experiment, one which I hope will serve its purpose, and that on the basis of the experience gained we shall know better how to use similar devices in the future.
May I answer the suggestions made by members of the New Democratic Party that we were seeking here a device for a particular purpose rather than a device for general application. We did look at the Swedish example but it did not seem to suit the purpose we had in mind. However, it is a useful device and I am sure that in the future we shall be looking for flexible instruments of this kind for general use in connection with fiscal and monetary policy.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to a proposal made by his party during the election campaign for some sort of deduction in respect of municipal taxes to give relief to home owners. We have examined this proposal and we find it neither equitable nor

I know that in the councils of our party during the election campaign we examined this proposal generally and we found that it was very inequitable as between home owners and the growing number of people who occupy rented accommodation. This is why we did not see fit to accept it at that time or include it in these budget proposals. It seemed to us that there were better ways of promoting home ownership.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I turn now to the general proposals which were advanced by various speakers as ways oi giving relief to taxpayers with lower incomes. In the first place, hon. members will have noticed that in the proposals now before the committee the government has left with the lower income taxpayers more of last year's tax cuts than it has with anyone else. This is some indication of our understanding of this problem and of our desire to moderate the effects of taxation on the lower income group.
Again, it is our opinion that it would have been most inadvisable at this time to have made any major changes in the structure of taxation until there has been an opportunity to study the recommendations of the Carter commission which are expected at any time. I do not believe that our present income tax is either as equitable or as efficient as it ought to be and I am hopeful that the Carter commission will recommend some fundamental changes both in methods of imposing taxes and in the structure of the taxes themselves. But until we receive those recommendations I do not think we should act to patch up the existing structure any more than we have done in recent years.
It is my view that nothing harms the position of the less favoured portion of this country more than general inflationary conditions. It is therefore very much in the interests of those parts of the country which have not been growing as rapidly as others that general inflationary pressure should be mitigated. So this budget, which is aimed directly at reducing excessive demand, is very much in the interests of those portions of the country where growth has not been as rapid as we would have wished. Anyone who suggests that we should allow inflation to become rampant in order to help the slow growth areas is obviously speaking economic nonsense.
A word about regional problems. The government has, of course, continued its policy of providing special incentives in the Atlantic region, in designated areas and other areas of slow growth. It has done so through measures of special assistance such as the Atlantic Development Board, and by the provision that the proposals for reduced capital cost allowances contained in the budget should not apply to the designated areas. I believe that the policies contained in the budget are very much in the interests of those areas of the country which are growing relatively slowly in relation to the remainder of Canada and I do not believe it would be helpful to

those areas if we were to allow inflationary pressures to go unchecked.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to intercede once again on behalf of the taxpayers of this country, the responsible, hardworking men and women who are caught in the cross-fire of high prices and high taxes which is beginning to wear them thin. I rose on March 25, prior to the introduction of the minister's budget, to plead at that time for special consideration for the Canadian breadwinner, the oppressed taxpayer and wage earner of this land, and I must say I was disappointed with the policies introduced by the minister in his budget so far as taxation relief for the average Canadian wage earner is concerned. I speak for the responsible Canadian man or woman who is appalled and even to a certain extent frightened by the economic forces currently conspiring against him. I refer to overspending, waste and extravagance at the official level and the apparent insensitivity to the mood and climate of this country at the level of the man on the street.
When I spoke on March 25 I said that many thousands of Canadian families and householders are casualties of a taxation and food price juggernaut that has been building up and rolling over them for the last several years, and I said they were looking for help to get out from under this crushing burden. I suggested that this is the price we pay for glorious legislative programs that go too far too fast. I reiterate that point of view today.
I do not for one moment disparage or minimize the importance of responsible social welfare, but I believe that to a certain extent the economic chickens are coming home to roost in Canada and we are reaping the whirlwind that we sowed when we sowed the wind of social legislation beyond our economic capacity. There comes a breaking point, and I suggest the time has now arrived for all of us in the chamber to ask ourselves whether or not we are straining the average wage earner too severely.
The current situation of labour unrest in this country is a reflection of a situation that we have created for ourselves, for our national self, by pursuing a program of social legislation that has exceeded the bounds of our economic capacity and social responsibility.

On every hand the government admonishes us to curtail expenditure, to curtail construction, to tighten our belts. Yet, as the leader of this party suggested earlier today, the government itself flouts its own instruction, while admonishing us to spend less, by devising, designing and proposing programs such as the massive monument to militarism envisaged for this city within the next few years.
At the time I spoke on March 25 I asked the minister if he would give consideration to the people who are caught in the price-tax squeeze by introducing three specific measures designed to relieve Canadians of these oppressive financial pressures. I repeat that I was indeed disappointed in the results of the budget, in the fact that it contained no such relief and in the fact that it contained little consideration or awareness that profound problems exist in those areas. I believe all of us in this chamber should warn ourselves that pride goeth before a fall. It behooves all of us in this chamber, not just the members on the treasury benches who are in the government but all members of the house, to realize that the problem does exist, is becoming increasingly acute, and that we must address ourselves to it.
I do not view it necessarily as a partisan problem and I do not believe in partisan solutions. I do not believe that any party in this chamber has a monopoly on solutions and answers to the problem. I urge a collective, massive, all-party assault on the sea of respectable poverty that exists today amidst our comparative affluence and prosperity.
I have been on the receiving end of a tremendous stream of letters on this subject. I know all hon. members receive letters on it daily, but I have a brief one here which I would like to read into the record because it symbolizes and typifies the plight of these nameless, faceless Canadians who are writing to all of us on this problem. Mr. Chairman, as I claim some interest in this legislation I should like to say a word on it. When the former minister, now Minister of National Health and Welfare, was in Vancouver last fall I arranged for him to meet with a number of vocational training students who were on unemployment insurance and were having a very difficult time under the existing program. The Minister of Labour met with these students in a small apartment in my riding. From that visit I think a good deal of the impetus in respect of this new program was developed.
Under this program, as the minister has explained, we will be paying 100 per cent of a $35 a week supplementary allowance and 90 per cent of an allowance of up to $55 a week to workers who are unemployed or to self-employed persons who were formerly in primary industry. This will mean a possible allowance of $90 a week to send these unemployed workers back to school for training or upgrading of their skills. I suggest, Mr. Vocational and Technical Training Chairman, that only one out of four or five of our young people will ever go to university. I think many of our politicians get carried away with the idea that we need more assistance to higher education and forget the great need which exists to look after the four out of five of our young people who never will see university.
Although I commend the government very much for bringing in this program, it does not make any provision for those young people who already are employed and who have some skill or semiskill but want to return to school either to re-train for another profession, another skill or another job or wish to upgrade their existing training. In this parliament some time ago we introduced the university loans program which I think proved to be overwhelmingly successful. In fact, there is a resolution on the order paper to increase the amounts under the university loans program. If we are going to look after those who wish to go back to vocational schools adequately many of whom are married and have dependant small children, it seems to me we should give serious thought to the establishment of a program for vocational training similar to the university loans program.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I do not think it would be difficult to establish a program under which young people who want to go back to vocational school to upgrade their training or receive new training could obtain a loan in the amount of $250 or $300 a month for a period of up to a year to enable them to enter into a comprehensive and complete retraining or vocational training program. The program we are considering now is a breakthrough with regard to the training of unemployed or underemployed persons, but I suggest there are many young people, married persons with family responsibilities, who are unable to go back to school and are unable to give up their jobs in order to retrain or upgrade themselves. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-194, to establish a corporation for the administration of the National Arts Centre.
She said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-194 provides for the management of the great building which will very soon grace the centre of our national capital. It constitutes an affirmation that we Canadians, like other mature and civilized people, are giving full recognition to the proper value of the performing arts in our society, not only here in Ottawa, our national capital, but throughout Canada.
Recently there was a Rockefeller panel report on the performing arts, and I should like to quote something that was stated therein:
The arts are a source of simple enjoyment and delight, hence of refreshment and renewal. They are also educating and civilizing, can provide a sense of grace, power, enchantment and beauty of which the creative impulse is capable. And, at their greatest, the arts are exalting, with some of religion's moral and mystical power.
There is no doubt in my mind about the prime importance that Canadians attach to the performing arts today. If there were, the collective experience of hon. members in this chamber, and particularly those who represent constituencies in our larger cities, would rapidly dispel it. The evidence is overwhelming and it comes from all parts of the country.
During the last 20 years, there have been steady progress in the development of the performing arts in Canada and it has assumed a sensible, and I think, logical pattern. First things have come first. Since the creation of the Canada Council in 1957, priority has been given to the development of strong professional companies with high artistic standards in their several fields. More recently, this movement has been accelerated by a growing volume of provincial and municipal support. In the last two or three years, we have entered a new phase, which has been

stimulated by the preparations for our centennial, but which I think would have developed naturally over the next few years in any event. There has been a gathering movement across the country, which has been felt very strongly of course in our larger cities where some facilities exist, to provide housing that will be worthy of the high standard of excellence of our leading artistic companies.
One of the happiest features of this development has been the passionate involvement of our young people. I have not myself seen it, but I have heard reports of the National Ballet School in Toronto, with its increasing numbers of young people dedicating their lives to the arts. I propose to visit this summer the summer camp of Les Jeunesses Musicales at lake Orford, in the eastern townships of Quebec, which many members have already taken the advantage of visiting. Experiences such as these are all that are needed to prove that the best of our young people are as talented and sound as ever, as ready as ever to accept the necessary discipline in achieving the mastery of beauty, just as this discipline is necessary to achieve anything which is worth having.
This measure before the chamber, then, Mr. Speaker, provides for the establishment of a corporation which will have three principal functions, first, to operate and maintain the centre; second, to develop the performing arts in the national capital region and, third, to assist the Canada Council in the development of the performing arts elsewhere in Canada. I shall come back to this in a moment, but it is important to keep in mind that there are three objects when we consider the structure which is proposed for the corporation.
The bill proposes a chairman, a vice chairman, five ex officio members and nine appointed members. The whole board will be concerned with the development and implementation of policy designed to achieve all three objects; but there is provision in clause 2 for the establishment of standing committees of the board to which duties may be delegated. In this way it will be possible to establish an executive committee which can give closer attention to the management and operations of the centre itself than could the full board.
The second object of the corporation, Mr. Speaker, is to develop in our national capital the performing arts. I am sure that many members, who over the years have regretted
June 9, 1966

June 9, 1966
National Arts Centre
are too small. I should like to stress the point that, in relation to the centre, we should not regard a subsidy as a means of meeting a deficit on operations. We do not regard the National Gallery or the National Museum as having a deficit on their operations. They are regarded as necessary amenities to the cultural life of Canada, and parliament votes money for their support. Exactly the same considerations should apply to the centre, which is not intended to be a commercial operation and cannot be expected to be selfsupporting from its revenues. Parliament will therefore be asked to provide funds for the objects of the corporation through the normal procedures for appropriations.
Finally, the bill provides that the corporation shall not be an agent of Her Majesty. In formulating and implementing its artistic policy, the board will have to make many difficult decisions, and will necessarily have to rely to a very large extent on the artistic judgment and taste of the director and its other advisers. As Emerson said, "Art is a jealous mistress", and it would be too much to expect unanimity of opinion about her qualities and virtue. We have to face the fact that the centre will not please everybody all the time. A lively artistic policy will be, in its very essence, controversial. The only policy that would not be controversial is the pursuit of mediocrity, and it would not be controversial only because it would be universally condemned.

Mr. Speaker,the other night when the resolution on this bill was presented, I was absent, with the other cultural types. I am afraid some of us missed the opportunity to comment on the National Arts Centre.
My own view is that we welcome the development of this centre. I know there are misgivings by some hon. members concerning the cost. However, I suggest that these thoughts should be expressed when the estimates of the Department of Public Works are before the house. In any case, I am not going to make a very great complaint about the cost of the centre. This country has waited for a long time for a centre of this type. Even at the inflated prices of today, I think the final result will be well worth while.
Last year in reply to a question I put on the order paper I found that since 1949 this country has spent something like $24 billion on defence. We may spend $100 million for some towers in the western part of Ottawa. It does not bother me that the government will spend the amount of money contemplated for the National Arts Centre. I think we have to do things of this sort.
It is disappointing that the centre will not be ready for the centennial year. We should not worry. If stretching out the construction period will save some cost, then not having it ready for the centennial year is not too serious. I am anxious to see that the job is well done, and if we have to wait until 1968 or 1969, I think it will be worth it. The centre will be with us for a very long time. I think of the famous opera houses in the major cities of Europe which have been in existence for 100 years, and are still being used at the
National Arts Centre
present time. Many of them are in very good condition because they were very fine structures initially.
In recent years there have been constructed in Canada a great many new auditoria, as well as theatres. I think of the Queen Elizabeth Theatre in Vancouver, the auditoria erected in Calgary and Edmonton, the Place des Arts in Montreal, the O'Keefe Centre in Toronto, the Confederation Memorial Theatre in Charlottetown, and the theatre at Stratford. All these have been built in the last ten years. There may be others of which I am not aware.
I suggest that these new buildings have resulted in a better environment for both the performing artists and for the audiences. For too long we have had symphony orchestras playing in motion picture theatres which were not designed for that purpose. We have had ballet and opera companies performing on stages which were just about half as big as they should have been. We have had various dramatic and theatrical groups playing on inadequate stages at high schools. These new buildings in Canada in recent years have provided much better physical facilities than we had before for the performing arts.
Not only have these new buildings improved conditions for the performers, but they have created a much better environment for the audience. I think of the change which took place in Vancouver when the Queen Elizabeth Theatre was opened. Before that time the various amateur dramatic and professional groups performed in old movie houses and in other halls. The type of audience they got was the hard core audience-the people who were going to keep supporting them so that the organizations would not collapse. I noticed that after the new theatre came into existence the audiences grew in size. The better lighting, better acoustics, more comfortable seating arrangement, the pleasant foyers where people could walk between acts all created a much more pleasant environment. Consequently the support for the various types of concerts and dramatic productions increased in the city. I imagine that the same thing happened in Calgary, Edmonton, Toronto and Montreal.
This situation of lack of facilities, Mr. Speaker, has been particularly prevalent in Ottawa. This city, which is quite close to Montreal and to Toronto, should get many of the travelling groups that go to those cities, but that do not stop here because of lack of facilities. I can recall on one occasion going

June 9, 1966
National Arts Centre
to see one company from New York which had to appear in a high school. Our whole evening was spoiled because a rock 'n roll dance was going on in the same building, and the dance music drowned out almost the whole act. This city has been badly served in the past with places in which theatrical groups could perform.
The buildings which I have mentioned, built in the other cities of Canada, in most cases are multi-purpose buildings. They were designed for operas, symphony concerts, theatrical productions and musical comedies. They had to be multi-purpose buildings because the people putting up the buildings did not have the money to provide more than one building at a time for the performing arts. This will not be so with the National Arts Centre. There are to be three buildings. The large hall is to seat 2,300 people, and is to be built for the presentations of ballet productions and can be used for symphonies. The other one will seat 970 people, and the smaller studio will seat 300. This is only possible, perhaps, where we have the federal government coming into the financial picture.
I am very pleased that we do not have to have a multi-purpose building-because it will be here for a long time-and it is much better to have the three buildings which are each adapted to a particular type of performance.
Some tribute ought to be paid, Mr. Speaker, to the group in Ottawa which did a great deal of the organizational work for the centre. I believe it is called the National Capital Council Arts Alliance, and is made up of 65 organizations. A great deal of consultation and planning went into the art centre, in order for it now to have reached this stage.
The site which has been selected I think is unfortunate. Two other sites were contemplated at the time, one on Sussex Street, and one on Albert Street. I felt that the one on Albert Street was the better of the two, but the former mayor of Ottawa vetoed that. If the centre represents a heavy cost, as related to the cost of excavating for parking areas, it is too late to put boulders back into the ground and move the site to another place. I think we should have had a great deal less cost at one of the other locations. As I recall, the planning director of the city at one time recommended against the present location, but it is too late to do anything now. The work has to go ahead.
I shall have something more to say, Mr. Speaker, when we come to the clauses of the bill. Now I should like to make a comment

about the composition of the board, the director, and the people who will advise the director.
I imagine that the board of trustees, as it is called, will be broadly representative geographically of the country, and I expect its members will be English and French speaking. I sometimes have my doubts about these boards of directors of national organizations. In many cases they are well intentioned prominent citizens, but unfortunately they do not know very much about the subject they are involved in, so that they have to do very much as the professionals suggest. In this case I suggest that there should be a board which is a mixture of people who may be quite prominent in the various fields of the arts, and other prominent citizens.
The centre has to be a business centre, too. There will be leases entered into, and there will be concessions. The board will probably need business advice. The key person, Mr. Speaker, will be the director. The type of person who has the artistic background combined with the ability to manage a business of this size is very hard to get.

I would suggest this: If we can get a Canadian, well and good. I would also suggest that the members of the advisory committees set up to assist the director in making plans for the operation of the centre will have a more important function than the board itself; they will be people who know the entertainment business and their advice will be extremely useful. The minister mentioned that it is planned to establish a permanent repertory company in the capital. I would refer to this later. It is hoped also that the symphony orchestra will be revived. Mr. Speaker, first I want to say a word to the minister, and I imagine my English speaking colleagues will realize in what bad position we are sometimes placed by the French language when we want to speak of such a charming lady and we have to refer to her as "Monsieur le ministre." You will understand that this is a sort of heresy that is distasteful to us, but to comply with the prescriptions of the French grammar, we must

refer to this charming person as "Monsieur le ministre".
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I am one of those who are happily impressed by the constructive influence of the present minister who is called the Secretary of State, but who plays the role of minister of culture in Canada.
For the short time she has been in office, we have seen for instance what happy results her influence had with regard to the National Gallery of Canada. I would simply want, at the beginning of my remarks, to express the hon. members' satisfaction for her constructive measures which enlightened us. The bill she has moved today proves that Canada has just reached maturity, since we can allow ourselves to forget prosaic preoccupations, such as roads or national defence, and awake to artistic values. Some thought had been given to it before, because the Canada Council has been established. That was a beginning, but now we are going to have a monument, a temple of the arts in Canada that we will be proud to show to those who will come here and realize that Canada, after a few centuries of existence, has just reached this maturity where it is intensively and successfully interested in things intellectual and artistic.
On the whole, Mr. Speaker, I find this bill particularly acceptable. All the same, I have a few remarks to make on a specific point, but before doing so, I wish to advise the house that I am making those remarks with all possible broad-mindedness, because I would not want to be accused of pettiness. But the fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that if a bill dealing with artistic and cultural matters in Canada is being introduced, it should be kept in mind that there are two main ethnic groups, two cultures working side by side to promote Canada's prosperity and, at the risk of seeming somewhat touchy, I wish to point out that I cannot find in this bill an adequate guarantee that my culture and that of a number of other members, as well as of a few million Canadians, will be administered, if I may use such a term, by people of my own language and culture.
If a few members find that to mention this on every occasion is to split hairs and to make a fanatic of oneself, I want to call their attention to one thing: we are too often reminded in our country that there are still some people-not only in the province of Quebec-who are fanatics and who tell us, as I read not later than this afternoon in the
June 9, 1966

report of a radio commentary, it is time French Canadians realized their language is unwelcome here in Canada. We are also told that Canada is a country with an English speaking majority and that French Canadians should realize they should adopt the language of the majority. This is only one step removed from telling us that we shall have to adopt the culture of the majority.
Indeed, I think that some members of the house object, for instance, to a French speaking radio station in Toronto-to which English speaking people are not compelled to listen. Now those are the things that prompt us to be vigilant. Anyhow, even if artistic and cultural matters have universal resemblances, even if art should not really be divided into compartments according to races-there is no French art, no English art, no Spanish art, no Italian art-nevertheless, there is in every nationality contingencies and characteristics which distinguish the culture and the art of each people.
I will not say any more about this, because I do not have the proficiency to do so; anyhow, members here understand as well as I do. But, Mr. Speaker, I think a minor amendment should be made to this bill.
Considering that directors having a diversified competence and who understand artistic matters will have to be appointed, we should make sure that they are also administrators.
