Mr. Speaker, I think there will be general support in the house for this particular bill, although the details may be examined when we reach the committee stage. I notice there have been some remarks of regret that the building to house the performing arts will not be ready for the centennial year. I do not share those regrets at all. I am beginning to worry about what Canada is going to do in 1968 and 1969. I do not think everything has to come to an end in 1967; in any case so far as the performing arts are concerned it will take time for these to become established and they scarcely will be ready by the time the building is completed.
I think this is a move in the right direction. There is a feeling in Canada with regard to the development of the performing arts, which are defined as the arts of the theatre and the concert hall, including the creating, staging and performing of drama, music and the dance. There may have been a time when the government or parliament as a whole need not have entered into this particular field, but with the advance of civilization we see that it is one of the essential factors of life to have some support for the performing arts, particularly in a country which has gone through such a long period of pioneering as has this country.
I speak with some feeling concerning this particular problem, because I have lived half my life in cities and half in the country and smaller towns. I know the difficulty which faces people living in the smaller areas of Canada who wish to receive adequate assistance and attention in the field of the performing arts. As a high school principal in a smaller town in Manitoba for a number of years, I had experience in this field. In the period of the depression, among other things we became ardent supporters of the excellent programs of the little theatre, which were sponsored by the then Governor General, Lord Bessborough, and we stimulated the theatrical interests in that smaller town.

I can think of high schools across this country which will look with interest on this particular development, because they will hope in the course of time to receive assistance as set out in the objects and powers of the corporation as contained in clause 9 which reads:
The objects of the Corporation are to operate and maintain the centre, to develop the performing arts in the national capital region and to assist the Canada Council in the development of the performing arts elsewhere in Canada.
It goes on to say they will arrange for and encourage some of these activities elsewhere than just in the capital city. There are hundreds of people across our country in scattered localities who look to the performing arts for guidance and assistance. In my own experience as a high school principal, I recall putting on seven one-act plays every year, plus an operetta, for a periood of about ten years. The difficulty in finding suitable one-act plays and operettas which could be adapted to high school students presented some problems. Because of the stimulus which will be afforded by this, in the long run all areas of Canada will benefit. It is not something which will happen overnight. But as the years go by we will develop in Canada an appreciation for the performing arts and for the people who are competent to participate in them. It can start at various levels throughout the country.
The time has long gone by when the people of Canada should have the advantage of performing arts only in major cities. We require travelling artists in this country in the field of music, in dance, and in theatrical performances to carry some of this excellent material which is available in the world to smaller localities. This has been one of the great weaknesses in our country over the years.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
I asked the minister a question when she completed her remarks and I should like to revert to that just for a moment. As I understood what the minister said, criticism and controversy might develop over some of the activities that might be carried on in the arts centre. Unless I misunderstood her, she considered that this might be advantageous. I want to present the point of view that in the field of the arts there should be a very limited attempt at stirring up controversy and criticism.
The example was given of the first performance at the Stratford Festival this year,
June 9, 1966

which aroused some adverse comment. This is inevitable. It depends I suppose on the producers of plays and festivals, who sometimes try to do things which are not readily acceptable to an audience. I have seen Shakespearean plays in Canada and in London, England, because I am an ardent theatregoer. I have seen Shakespearean plays presented in London in modern dress because somebody thought this was the way it should be done. I enjoy a Shakespearean play in the costumes of the Elizabethan period much more than I did the one I saw in modern dress; but the producer thought that he would bring things up to date.
However, in the field of the lasting good things in the performing arts there is no real controversy. Shakespeare's plays have endured for three centuries. The works of Gilbert and Sullivan are still enjoying great popularity and it does not require major change to make those operettas acceptable. The great play "Oklahoma" did not arouse controversy; it was not needed, because there was the interest in "Oklahoma" right from the start. "My Fair Lady" has run for years in the live theatre and on television. Interest and appreciation are there, but no stimulus of controversy.
In the field of the opera, some of the operas have a long history behind them and are performed year after year to the great enjoyment of audiences. In the field of ballet there is no controversy aroused. It is an examination of the excellence of the production that interests an audience. In the field of music, which fortunately crosses all barriers of language, again it is the question of excellence and appreciation that people are considering. So I hope that in this project, in which there will be a great deal of interest we will not, certainly in the early stages-I do not suppose it can be avoided altogether-attempt to stir up public interest by putting on performances in the arts centre that are a little out of the ordinary or are calculated to make people think.
We have been subjected to enough of that type of thing on radio and television to last us for the rest of our lifetime, and for two or three more lifetimes, by people who get the idea that the general populace is not thinking enough about some problem that is stirring around in the mind of some writer, play producer or interviewer. The theatre, ballet, the philharmonic orchestra-I have always gone to these performances for relaxation and enjoyment and the higher the standard
National Arts Centre
of performance, the better I like it. I do not rule out the comedy by any means. I like to have a good laugh. But I do not go to these performances in order to be made to think about some major problem that is affecting the world. I just express my earnest hope that we will be saved from that type of experiment in the performing arts centre. Life has enough problems without having additional ones forced upon us by the theatre or television.
Let us get some reasonable enjoyment out of our relaxation. If the development of talent is emphasized, then we do not need to worry about controversial aspects. If standard of excellence is the object, then I think the populace generally will be satisfied.
May I just say that we have a great opportunity here to develop Canadian culture. Perhaps I should not have used that term. We have a great opportunity to develop in Canada a populace that will appreciate culture. "Culture" is a badly misused word and I am using it in the context of the bill before us. We have here a great opportunity to develop an appreciation of the theatre, of the dance, of music. As I head one adjudicator say at a music festival, the object of the festival is to pace each other on the road to excellence. Everything does not have to be highbrow; you can stand only so much of that. But there are degrees of taste in the arts, and the centre must accommodate itself to them.
For those who like classical music, that should be provided For those who have less appreciation of classical music, some of the other types of music would have to be provided. Similarly with theatrical productions; there will be, I hope, an adequate variety for the various tastes in our country. But the opportunity is here now to develop across this country an appreciation of some of the finer things of life. There is a tremendous heritage in these three fields. We are so fortunate in having in our country representatives of almost every known racial group in the world whose appreciation, knowledge of and talent in the performing arts is very widespread. It is not restricted to any one racial group; it is virtually spread right across all racial groups.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
No country other than the United States has the wealth of talent available to it that Canada has, because of the millions of people in Canada from so many different cultural

June 9, 1966
National Arts Centre
backgrounds who have brought over to this country from Europe an interest in music and the arts, which has been of great assistance to us. The opportunity is really tremendous. I think that through this arts centre we can shake ourselves free from too great a dependence upon radio and television programs that come from the United States. I do not for a minute think that we can develop our own culture from within our own ranks, but we will be able to develop talented people in this country and retain them here, instead of losing them to the United States. Perhaps in time we will be able to attract talented people from the United States and other countries of the world to live here in Canada and play their parts in developing the performing arts in our country. With careful attention given to the objectives of the corporation that is proposed, and with reasonable attention given to the amount of money that is invested in this corporation, I think we will have an opportunity to develop something very useful in Canada.
I think we should be a little careful about the expenditure of money because if we go too far too fast it can be a wasteful process. I would like to see the corporation develop a program which will bear fruit in several years time and will rest on a sound foundation, without becoming extravagant.
Finally, may I revert to what I said at the beginning. I do hope that the smaller areas of Canada will receive attention and benefit from the corporation for the performing arts. I think that people who live and work in the smaller areas of Canada deserve greater attention in this particular field than they have received in the past. I trust that not only the major cities of Canada will receive the attention of this corporation, but that it will keep in mind the smaller locations throughout the country.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to make a few remarks about this bill. Needless to say that, like most of my colleagues, I support its principle which is to stimulate the development of the arts in Canada.
However, I would like to recall the remarks made a little earlier by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres about the representation of French Canadians on that government agency. Once again we are faced with the establishment of a crown corporation, another ramification, another arm of centralization in a field which, in my opinion, should respect the provincial authority more.
If I am not mistaken, culture falls to a large extent under provincial jurisdiction and, more particularly, under the responsibility of regional and municipal governments. Instead of establishing a corporation such as this one and, as I said, without being against the principle of this bill, I feel that a coordinating agency should have been created whose function would have been precisely to give the essential services to the various regions of Canada and particularly to take greater interest in the population of small municipal centres, urban or rural, who are not fortunate enough to travel to the large centres to take part in artistic events.
And, Mr. Speaker, that is the defect of the proposed corporation. If I refer to the bill, it seems very obvious that the coporation's main objective is to create in the city of Ottawa an arts centre which will, in fact, fill a gap the city of Ottawa itself has not remedied.
In Montreal we created the Place des Arts which gives wonderful opportunities to artists; but the Place des Arts was created and financed with money from the municipal and provincial governments. As far as I know, the federal authorities did not contribute anything to the development of that cultural centre.
And I am wondering why today-and, as I said before, I am not criticizing the objective-the federal government should make a giit to a city which did not fulfill its obligations in that field? Apparently that is all there is to it.
It is obvious-and the minister should admit it-that people will not travel from Toronto,
June 9. 1966

Montreal or even more remote areas to attend an artistic event in Ottawa. What we need to develop culture and the arts in Canada is to give the small municipalities the regions remote from large centres, the facilities and means to develop the arts locally.
Think of the artists who brought fame to our country through their talent and you will often find that the most promising artists come precisely from regions remote from the large centers.
How can we efficiently help those artists who live in communities not too remote from great centres to develop if we do not give them the proper facilities to do so, without incurring extraordinary if not impossible expenses. That is somewhat the meaning of my remarks.
Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat that we should specify in the bill the representation that French Canadians will have and on which they may count. This bill, as all bills of this nature, is very vague and I think the minister should take a position more clearly on this and tell us that she intends to respect essential standards so as to ensure adequate French Canadian representation on the board of trustees of the corporation.
The minister should also tell us whether the government has already approached people for the position of director of this centre, and if so, I believe it would be in the interest of the corporation to know who those people are.
Mr. Speaker, parliament should have a say in the selection of the staff of crown corporations because it happens unfortunately too often that governments introduce legislation and set up standards for a corporation, when we know very well, by tradition, that certain persons have been approached beforehand. It would be unfortunate if political favouritism were to play in the case of a legislative measure such as this one. I do not want to make a charge but it would be unfortunate if that happened-it does sometimes-because the board of trustees of the arts centre should be free of all political partisanship.
I think the minister should, considering the interest created by this bill, tell us what representation and participation, minimum or statutory, if one prefers, will be provided for French Canadians on the board of this corporation. I think also that it should be stipulated in the bill that a preference must be given to Canadian artists, which it does not now.
National Arts Centre
Naturally, art knows no borders but it Canadians are called upon to spend tremendous funds for the development of arts in Canada, I think it is natural for us to insist even more on Canadian artists having a preference in the distribution of expenses which will be made to set up this centre.
1 also believe, Mr. Speaker, that we should have foreseen the foundation of opera companies made up of Canadian artists. A Canadian opera company is lacking in Canada. Yet, we have plenty of home talent. Everyone interested in the arts complains that we are still without a Canadian opera company. We have local companies which often have to balance their budgets with contributions from their members and I believe the Canadian government should do more to help such companies integrate with larger organizations.
For some time there has been talk of creating an opera company in Montreal. Unfortunately, the authorities have recently advised us that such an undertaking would not be a paying proposition because expenses would be too great.
To my mind, if this bill provided instead for the establishment of a co-ordinating body for the arts, in Canada, it would be much more helpful and could assist all those organizations, groups, companies, and artists. Such a project would be more helpful to assess the needs of those people and help them to increase their contribution to Canadian culture.
I hope that the minister will keep these remarks in mind. I want her to know that even if in principle I approve the purpose of the bill, once again I deplore that this body should be contrary to my understanding of a definition of the British North America Act, a responsibility that comes under provincial jurisdiction. The central government exists to assist the provinces in areas where they are unable to meet the needs on their own. I think that here again, there is an infringement-possibly indirect, into the field of education, but I believe the minister would have been better advised to establish a coordinating body which would have worked hand in hand with the provincial governments and the latter could then have cooperated with the municipal authorities in areas far removed from the large centres for the advancement of the arts in Canada and to give us better representation in the artistic field.

National Arts Centre

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments on the bill, the purpose of which is to my mind most praiseworthy, namely to have a National Arts Centre. I must also point out, however, that this federal initiative goes squarely against the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution.
I would like the hon. Secretary of State to tell us on the strength of what section of the Canadian constitution, which as far as 1 know still applies, the federal government is allowed to enter the field of national arts centres without having previously discussed the matter with the provinces, obtained their agreement, their co-operation and consensus.
In 1867, the Canadian constitution, in section 93, stipulated that the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction in relation to education the word "exclusively" being used in the constitution. It is needless to give the definition of the word "exclusive" to the house. Later on various interpretations were given, for example that of Justice Duff of the Superior Court who decided in one case that the word "education" in section 93 was to be interpreted in its widest sense, meaning primary, secondary and university education, and also in the field of culture, and this, in spite of the beating around the bush of the Massey-Levesque Commission on culture.
Even so, the resolutions of the 1864 Quebec Conference, on which are based the 147 sections of the Canadian constitution, did not separate the fields of university and culture from the "field of education". And now the central government continues to take initiatives on its own, without consulting the provinces, reaching an agreement with them, or co-operating with them.
I understand that nine Canadian provinces have probably no objection to the interference of the central government in various fields and agree that the central government should establish standards in the financial and economic fields as well as in connection with arts.
The province of Quebec firmly objects to that procedure, because it is useless to repeat the well-known argument to the effect that Quebec is the stronghold of the French Canadian nation and has a special conception of arts. Now, the province of Quebec wants to establish its standards according to its cultural, educational and artistic conception.
For that purpose there is a Department of Cultural Affairs. Why then, has the Secretary

of State (Miss LaMarsh) considered the establishment of a National Arts Centre without previously reaching an agreement with the representatives of the province of Quebec, in order to associate the provincial Department of Cultural Affairs with the creation of that organization?
Well, I repeat, as I have said since the beginning of the session, that it is because everything is done backwards. This creates tensions, problems and misunderstanding among Canadians from Halifax to Vancouver. This is why it is urgent, Mr. Speaker, in that field like in many others, it is advisable to determine the constitutional, political, economic, financial, cultural and artistic responsibilities between the central and provincial governments. This cannot be done at the present time under the procedure followed by a central government which is always unilaterally acting to invade completey a field and then, having determined the standards and received its full share of the tax revenue, spends the funds in fields which, under the constitution, fall within the provincial jurisdiction.
Well, the only way, Mr. Speaker, would be to authorize parliament, the House of Commons, to institute a joint parliamentary committee-we often bring up the subject and will continue to do so until this government finally accepts to determine responsibilities as is reasonable in this important matter. This is the only way to eliminate tensions and lack of understanding between Canadians in all provinces, between different cultures and different ethnic groups; that is why I reject the principle of this bill which is similar to other bills introduced by this government.
A few weeks ago the government introduced a bill concerning the National Science Council. There again, the consent of the provinces was not first obtained nor was there any previous agreement. Well, Mr. Speaker, I find it unfortunate that this federal government continues to act in this way, which is the best way to maintain the existing chaos, tensions and lack of understanding between Canadians.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
This criticism is not addressed personally to the hon. Secretary of State, a very nice and charming person, but to the attitude and policy of this government which we have seen in action from the beginning of the session and which is aware of the existing tensions, as pointed out in the first report of
June 9, 1966

National Arts Centre
the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. We wish to stress the fact that this first report, in spite of press criticism in certain provinces, indicated that tensions and a serious crisis in the country do exist, originating in the province of Quebec. Why? Because the province of Quebec has different views on those subjects, as on many others, and this, not for the sake of being different from other provinces, but because it is respectful of the Canadian constitution.
When Quebec representatives raise such points we are proud of it, not because we feel we are giving rise to unruliness throughout the country, but because we build upon a confederative pact entered into in 1867, While we apply ourselves in several circumstances to violate its main provisions, as well as its spirit.
I hope, therefore, that the bill will be referred to a committee which will be able, in the course of its discussions, to agree on the establishment of a parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution.
This evening, we are dealing with a National Arts Centre. In two weeks, it will be another unilateral piece of legislation. This is not the way to settle the differences and the problems in our country. It would be so easy to solve them by asking responsible people, the representatives of the people in this house, to meet around a table in a parliamentary committee in order to exchange views, to define and determine responsibilities, and then to discuss matters with other provinces, such as the province of Quebec which precisely set up a parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution two years ago that will probably submit its report within a few months.
Mr. Speaker, I hope these remarks have been well received and will produce some results.

I should like to say a few words. I have heard much discussion in the house tonight, and I believe it can be said that many Canadians of many origins are very proud that there should be a centre for the performing arts in the national capital.
A great many people feel that the present minister is as good a person as can be put in the charge of such a project. Many feel that she is not making culture into a thin sort of thing, for only a fringe of people who are apt to turn up their noses at what a great many
other people classify as culture. I believe that large sections of the people want to be included in the benefits arising out of this centre.
I do not think it should be necessary to go into a whole lot of constitutional questions when speaking about this project. It will be good to have the arts centre established in this capital city as a result of a government measure. What does concern me is how the greatest use may be made of the centre. In my view it should be shared by the citizens of this country from coast to coast. In Ottawa there is a tendency to make a show window of all the beautiful things we have, forgetting that there are many people across the country who, even with the best means of transportation, will never see or use any of our facilities.
We ought to consider ways and means of sharing this National Arts Centre as broadly as we can among the people. It is important that the resources of this centre should be used to build regional centres, and regional arts across Canada. That should be part of its function. However, I do not think we should delay the building of this National Arts Centre until every little spot in Canada has a regional centre. In other words, I think we ought to find ways and means of making the benefits of the National Arts Centre available to the Canadian people.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
A few years ago the treasurer of the art gallery began sending travelling exhibitions of paintings across this country. These reached a good many of the smaller centres in this country, and I know the people living in these places much appreciated the opportunity to see these works of art. In years gone by some of our big stores would obtain a single painting and make it a centre of attraction to be seen, over a period of weeks, by very large numbers of people. June 9, 1966
National Arts Centre
I do not live in one of the most remote parts of Canada. In Vancouver, where I live, the people appreciate many of the fine television performances which the C.B.C. has made available. Let us make generally available the best that is done in the performing arts centre.
There is bound to be a great deal of criticism about the amount spent on this centre. I believe this criticism would be justified only if the centre is shut away, to be enjoyed by relatively few people. But there will be no justification for this criticism if we use the radio, television and travelling companies to make available to Canadians right across this country the benefits which arise from the founding of such a centre as this. This would be the best way of countering the hostile criticisms we have heard tonight about guaranteeing cultural rights. It would be the best way to effect Canadian unity.

[Mrs. Maclnnls.l

I think he is showing a rather too drastic attitude when he says that the whole field of culture is exclusively under provincial jurisdiction. Mr. Speaker, the right solution here does not only reside in the fact that the federal government can introduce the kind of bills we are now considering but in going further still to create a cultural affairs division which could be under the Department of the Secretary of State and have the special task of promoting French culture outside Quebec, because if French culture is restricted to the province of Quebec, I do not see how separatism will not one day make greater strides than at the present time. I entirely agree with the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) when she introduces such bills, because in my opinion, the federal government must undertake to spread French culture outside Quebec. This is the only way to achieve a truly Canadian culture and tongue.

It seems to me that culture is one field in which narrowmindedness and intolerance should not enter. I do not think the day will ever come when tolerance and understanding will have to be legislated. Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words with respect to this amendment. As I understand it, if this amendment passes, the members of the board would be composed of people who represent the two cultures of Canada. Bilingualism has that connotation at this time. That is my understanding. I think that this would be the worst type of discrimination which could be entered on the statute books of this country. After all, there are some six million Canadians who have ethnic backgrounds other than French or English, who are proud to be Canadians, who want to participate in the cultural life of this country, and who have a great deal to offer, both in culture and in tradition, by way of stimulating our country now and for the future.
June 9, 1966

By this amendment I feel that these people would be discriminated against. If they had the ability, and it was recognized that they would make good members of the board and would have something to add, this amendment would entirely eliminate them from consideration. This would be a crying shame, and any action of this sort by this parliament would tend only to divide the country more.
I have been listening to debates in this house for a number of years now and particularly during the past year or so we have been engaging here, by actions of this nature, in practices which are disuniting the country more than ever before. What we should be doing, irrespective of whether we are of French origin, English origin or any other origin, is working together as Canadians, all for the benefit and good of this country.
I am not suggesting that we must have representation on certain boards of certain ethnic groups. What I am suggesting is that we are all Canadians, and that we have the ability, the knowledge and the willingness to go forward and build up the country, whether culturally or any other way. We should all be recognized and no distinction should be made in this manner.
I must vote against this amendment, Mr. Chairman, because I do not think it gives a fair opportunity to every Canadian who wants to be Canadian, has proved himself to be a Canadian, and who wants to work for the Canadian way of life.

I rise at this time, Mr. Speaker, to discuss a question I put to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration a few days ago. Mr. Speaker did not permit my question to be answered at that time. Since then I have inquired whether the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration asked for an inquiry to be conducted into the winter works program undertaken by certain municipalities, notably, Notre Dame de la Guadeloupe, St. Ephrem de Beauce, and St. Methode de Frontenac.
Winter works projects go back to 1961. Although the minister has written to me that the inquiry would be undertaken, I should like to know when it is to take place. Is it to take place under federal or provincial jurisdiction, and will the federal or provincial authorities make the investigations. I shall await patiently for the outcome of such an inquiry.
It might be wise if the minister would ask the members of the unemployment insurance office in St. Georges de Beauce about a man known as Mr. Donalcourt, who made an inquiry last year respecting the proceedings in the municipality of St. Ephrem de Beauce. This inquiry was quite lengthy, and contains revealing facts about which the minister
[Mr. Prittie.l
would be interested. I might point out that the Unemployment Insurance office in St. Georges de Beauce found it necessary to make its own inquiry into the questions I have raised.
The minister would also find it useful to look at the correspondence between the Minister of Finance last year, the former member for Beauce, and the minister of labour of that time, respecting certain allegations to do with the municipality of St. Ephrem de Beauce. The allegations are similar to those having to do with the municipalities of Notre Dame de la Guadeloupe and St. Methode de Frontenac.
May I point out that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) could benefit from such an inquiry. I know that the hon. member for Beauce would favour obtaining up to date facts about the municipalities in question. He is still mayor of St. Honore de Shenesey which is six miles away from some of these municipalities and he might be able to explain some of the proceedings which have been going on.
I do not wish to press the matter further. I just wanted to make these few observations and ask the minister whether he does not wish to take account of this inquiry which has been made at the employment office about Mr. Donalcourt. I would point out that tomorrow, I believe, we shall be dealing with motions for the production of papers, asking for papers connected with that inquiry. maintopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-SMOKING-REQUEST FOR CONTROL MEASURES
HEALTH AND WELFARE-SMOKING-REQUEST FOR CONTROL MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on orders of the day on May 31 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare if he was aware of the fact that the government of B.C. declared that day to be non-smoking day in B.C., in line with his campaign to combat lung cancer, heart disease, and other kindred problems. The Speaker ruled my question out of order, and in consequence I asked that I be allowed to bring it up again on this occasion.
My reason in asking the question was to draw the attention, not only of the minister and of the House of Commons but of the entire country to the continuing toll taken in human life by the consumption of cigarettes, and to draw attention to the need for the federal government and all people at the federal level to do more than has been done so far to reduce this toll.
Along with several other hon. members, I am active in trying to promote measures to improve traffic safety and safety features in automobiles. That is a worthwhile endeavour, but I think there is a greater need for us to concern ourselves with the toll and slaughter taken by the consumption of cigarettes in Canada. In that regard, in my opinion I can do no better that quote briefly from some of the statements made by the health department of the government of B.C. on the cigarette disease toll:
Throughout Canada in 30 years deaths from lung cancer have multiplied by 1,500 per cent to a record level of over 2,000 deaths per year.
The Canadian Medical Association shows that cancer and smoking have been linked together for the past 100 years . . .
This year in Canada more than 2,750 people will die from lung cancer, almost twice the combined deaths from all the infective and parasitic diseases, including tuberculosis.
Dr. Michael B. Shimkin, a cancer specialist with the United States national institute of health, referring to the rising tide of evidence showing the menace of cigarette smoking said:
Were we speaking of spinach, the selling of spinach would now be a capital offence.

He went on to say:
Cigarettes should be regarded as a major environmental poison.
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of hon. members and the Chair I could quote at great length on this subject, but this is not the time to do so. I wish to point out just one other fact. People who smoke cigarettes regularly and in high number have a 50 per cent greater chance of dying from heart problems then those who do not smoke. I should like to conclude the quotation from the declaration of the health department of British Columbia with the statement that what is needed and needed very desperately is federal action toward guidance and support at the national level to combat the incidence of disease from cigarette smoking.
In conclusion I should like to pose the following question: Does the government of Canada, through its Department of National Health and Welfare, really believe it is doing enough to combat this disease which is related to cigarette smoking and which has been found to exist not only by the British Columbia health department, but also our own Department of National Health and Welfare, the United States health department, the British health department, the Scandinavian health department and the Russian health department? I think we should do a great deal more than we have done. I sincerely urge the government to examine the situation and try to step up their campaign against cigarette smoking by employing different means. Will the government do this?

DEFENCE PRODUCTION-INQUIRY AS TO DESTROYER ESCORT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow the parliamentary secretary, who is an adjoining neighbour of mine in New Brunswick. As of now I imagine the parliamentary secretary will be taking over part of the constituency which I represent. I should not like my friends in New Brunswick to misunderstand me if I were to say we were the only two in this house, but there are not many more.
The matter to which I should like to refer tonight has reference to a question I asked last Tuesday, June 7. I mentioned the lay-off of 600 men in the Saint John shipbuilding industry, and I asked the Minister of National Defence whether he had any up to date information on the present position in respect of the naval program; that is, the program for four new destroyers and two supply ships which he mentioned some months ago. It is quite true that I should have referred this matter, perhaps, to the Minister of Industry whose department, the Department of Defence Production, has the final responsibility for the construction of vessels of this nature. However, I have had very poor luck lately with the Department of Industry. We cannot get Saint John moving into the incentive program. We lost the Bonaventure through misadventure or some other circumstance, and we are being hard hit in the maritimes, particularly in Saint John, by the Department of Industry.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I noticed in the paper that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) has a great deal of money to spend, hundreds of millions of dollars, and felt I might appeal to him and ask whether, with regard to the four vessels which are to be constructed, there might be a chance that on some basis this work could be distributed around the shipyards on the east coast, which would include Saint John.
I suggest that this is a matter of serious concern to our community because 600 men will be lost to the industry forever. They are skilled and have been in the trade for some time. They will go elsewhere in this transformation period, when construction work is scarce in our shipping industry. Surely we are entitled to know where we fit into the plans that are being put into being.

I recall that in 1962 announcements were made that there were to be built a number of new destroyer escorts, or general purpose frigates, and this program has been postponed for various reasons up to this time. I call on the government to give us this information. Let us know what we can expect; whether these men should stick around in the hope that something might be forthcoming.
I am very critical of the Department of National Defence. They have virtually wiped out our poor old navy, and I make this appeal: Don't do the same to the shipbuilding industry, which is so important to a community such as ours in Saint John. I see the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) in his place. I thank him very much for staying here at this late hour. I hope he will be able to give us some encouragement that this program is now finally moving ahead, and that we can expect a tender call with some sort of allocation very soon.
